1.blurb: Mongol Empire tells the story of the steppe army from the inside — how Temüjin united the feuding clans of Mongolia around 1206 and forged the most effective military machine of the medieval world, the force that fell on the Rus'.
Mongol Empire follows the conquests that built that empire and, in later chapters, its split into four khanates — including the one that would rule Russia from the lower Volga.

Kievan Rus' tells the destruction of Kiev from the victim's side — the end of the brilliant river-civilization the Mongols broke, and the same Franciscan friar reporting a city reduced to a field of bones.

Kievan Rus' covers that civilization at its height under Yaroslav the Wise — Saint Sophia, the Golden Gate, birchbark letters, and the gold-ground icons — so you can measure the scale of what was lost.

2.blurb: Mongol Empire explains the Horde's place inside the larger empire — it was the ulus (inheritance) of Jochi, Genghis's eldest son — and traces the conversion of its rulers to Islam that opened a religious gulf with the Orthodox Rus'.

Mongol Empire shows the same administrative machinery — census-based taxation and a postal relay system borrowed from China — running from Russia to Persia to the steppe, not a uniquely Russian imposition.
Kievan Rus' opens the same saint-versus-collaborator debate from the Kievan side — Nevsky beating the Swedes and the Germans, then kneeling to the Horde and enforcing its census on his own people.

3.blurb: Mongol Empire tells the 1327 Tver episode from the conqueror's side: Tver kills the Horde's tax party, Ivan Kalita leads the punitive army, and is rewarded with the yarlyk and the right to collect everyone's tribute — the hinge of Moscow's rise.

Mongol Empire traces the plague's road in detail — out of Asia, through the Genoese colony of Caffa in 1346, ravaging the Golden Horde's own territories — the same trade corridor that carried it up into the Russian forest by 1352.
Kievan Rus' notes the Orthodox metropolitan relocating north from ruined Kiev, the move that this chapter narrates in full as the Church's spiritual capital settles on Moscow.

4.blurb: Mongol Empire names and dates the same Horde crisis — twenty khans in twenty years after 1359 — the collapse from the steppe side that let Dmitry risk open battle at Kulikovo.

Timurid Empire tells the full story of the Central Asian world-conqueror who would soon smash Tokhtamysh and wreck the Horde's cities, doing far more damage to Moscow's overlord than any Russian army.

Byzantine Empire covers the living late-Byzantine artistic tradition that Theophanes carried north into Russia — the gold-ground icon world that Andrei Rublev would inherit and make unmistakably Russian.

5.blurb: Timurid Empire narrates Timur's destruction of the Horde and the fragmentation that followed into the Kazan, Astrakhan, Crimean, and Great Horde successor khanates — the cracking of the power that held the yoke.

Kievan Rus' anatomizes the same Rurikid succession flaw — the brother-to-brother "ladder" system that fragmented the Kievan world, the structural defect Moscow inherited and nearly destroyed itself over.

Ottoman Empire tells the conquest of Constantinople from the victor's side — the cannon and the siege that ended a thousand years of Byzantium and, to Moscow, seemed to leave it the last free Orthodox power on earth.
Byzantine Empire covers the fall from the victim's side — the last emperor dying in the breach — the catastrophe that seeded Moscow's claim to inherit the imperial crown.

6.blurb: Byzantine Empire traces the Palaiologos dynasty and the scattering of its survivors into Western exile after 1453 — the imperial line whose niece Ivan III married, claiming the Byzantine inheritance for Moscow.

6.blurb: Mongol Empire tracks the disintegration of the Horde into squabbling successor states that made the bloodless standoff on the Ugra possible — the long fade behind the conventional 1480 end-date of the yoke.

Kievan Rus' documents the older Slavic ranks of unfreedom — the kholopy (slaves) and tribute-owing peasants — the legal ancestors of the serfdom that the Sudebnik's St. George's Day clause begins to build here.

7.blurb: Russian Empire opens on the inheritance of this very title — "Tsar" from "Caesar," the Byzantine imperial claim that Ivan IV makes formal in 1547 and that Peter will trade for the Western "Emperor" two centuries later.
Mongol Empire lists these two Volga states among the fragments the Golden Horde shattered into — the very Tatar successor khanates that Russia, the former tributary, now turns and conquers.

8.blurb: Russian Empire develops the Crimean slave-raiding economy that drove these horsemen north for captives by the tens of thousands — the same Horde-fragment khanate that burned Moscow to the ground in 1571.
Russian Empire carries forward the eastward expansion begun here with Yermak — the conquest of all Siberia to the Pacific, set in motion by the defeat of this Tatar khanate beyond the Urals.

11.blurb: Russian Empire treats this same 1649 law code as the moment that "finished a long process of binding the Russian peasant" — this chapter is the fuller account of how the binding was made total and hereditary.

Kievan Rus' sets up the contested inheritance behind this 1654 oath — how the old Kievan lands fell to Lithuania and Poland, producing the Russia-Ukraine-Belarus divergence that Pereyaslav reopened and that is argued over to this day.

12.blurb: Russian Empire opens on this same 1682 massacre — the musketeers storming the Kremlin before the boy Peter's eyes — the scene where the Muscovy book ends and the imperial book begins.

Russian Empire re-tells Peter's western apprenticeship — the shipyards of Amsterdam and Deptford, the hired specialists — as the opening of its own story, the same reign seen as the birth of the empire rather than the end of Muscovy.

Russian Empire picks up exactly here, at the 1721 Treaty of Nystad and Peter taking the imperial title — the seam where the Tsardom of Muscovy ends and the two centuries of empire reaching from Poland to the Pacific begin.
